desc:
Contract review summaries and key term flags turn long agreements into short, readable pages for your team. Ecom Swift LLC builds a review step that pulls out parties, dates, renewal and payment terms and marks unusual clauses for a person to check.

## What are contract review summaries?

A contract review summary is a plain-English page that sits beside the original agreement. It states who the parties are, what each side must do, when the contract starts and ends, how renewal works, what the payment terms are and which clauses look unusual. Every point is marked so a person can confirm it against the source text.

This is a reading aid for your team. It is not legal advice, and it does not replace a lawyer. It helps you decide which contracts need a lawyer's attention, and what to ask.

## Why contracts get signed without being fully read

Most businesses hold more agreements than anyone has time to study: supplier terms, client agreements, leases, software subscriptions, service level documents. Under pressure, people skim the first page and sign. The costly details sit later, such as an automatic renewal with a short notice window, a payment term longer than expected, or a clause that limits what you can claim if something goes wrong.

Those details only matter when a date arrives or a dispute starts, and by then the contract is in a drawer. A structured summary brings the details forward to the moment you can still act on them.

## How summaries improve decisions and follow-up

When key terms sit in one page and one sheet, comparing contracts becomes practical. You can see which suppliers renew automatically, which clients have the longest payment terms and which agreements share the same unusual clause. Renewal and notice dates become entries in a calendar instead of surprises.

Review time falls because a person reads the flagged parts first, not every paragraph in order. Quality improves because the same checklist is applied to every contract, rather than depending on who happened to read it and how tired they were. The summaries are only as good as the checklist, so we build it with you.

## What a useful review includes

- A one-page summary in everyday language, with no dense legal phrasing repeated back.
- Parties, signing date, start date, term and end date listed clearly.
- Payment terms, invoicing rules and late payment clauses extracted.
- Renewal, notice and termination conditions written out with their dates.
- A check against your own list of terms that matter to you, such as exclusivity or liability limits.
- Unusual or one-sided clauses highlighted with the page or section reference.
- A short list of questions you may want to put to your lawyer.
- A dates sheet that can feed calendar entries and reminders.
- A clear note on what the summary does not cover.

## How we work

First we read two or three of your typical contracts and ask what you most worry about. From your answers we draft a checklist and a one-page layout, and you adjust both. We then run the review on your documents and mark every extracted item with its location in the original.

The Basic package covers a small batch with a summary and key term list for each. Standard applies your own checklist, collects renewal and notice dates and adds a questions list for your lawyer. Premium gives your team a reusable template, calendar entries for key dates and a side-by-side comparison of versions, with a short guide to using it safely. A person on your side should always confirm important points before relying on them.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Confirm each flagged term against the original text before acting on it.
- Pass anything high value or unusual to a qualified lawyer.
- Put notice dates in a shared calendar with a warning well ahead of time.
- Use the same checklist for similar contracts so they can be compared.
- Keep signed originals in one known place.

**Avoid:**
- Treating a summary as a legal opinion.
- Skipping the original on contracts with large financial exposure.
- Letting renewal dates sit unrecorded.
- Asking the review to judge whether a clause is fair, since that is a legal question.
- Sending contracts to anyone without agreeing how they will be stored.

## Who this service is for

It suits a small business owner with a folder of supplier agreements and no time to read them all. It suits an agency that signs similar client contracts and wants renewal dates tracked. It also suits an office manager preparing for an audit or a change of provider, who needs to see current obligations at a glance.

## What we need from you

Send the contracts you want reviewed, your list of terms that matter and any past issues you want to avoid. Tell us how confidential the documents are, and we will work inside the folder or workspace you choose. We never ask for passwords. Access is given by sharing a folder or inviting us as a collaborator, and you can remove that access when the work ends.
